common_name: Admiral African Violet (Historic Original Ten Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Admiral was among the original ten African violet cultivars introduced into American commerce by Armacost & Royston in the late 1920s.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in moist propagating mix and grow on as a houseplant in bright indirect light, never direct sun, in slightly acidic, well-drained potting mix. Admiral carries single, rich violet-blue flowers over a compact rosette of dark, quilted foliage, a color and form typical of the wild-derived selections distributed before decades of hybridizing produced the ruffled, double, and fantasy-patterned cultivars common today. As one of the founding original ten cultivars, it is grown today mainly by collectors and society members interested in African violet history rather than for show-bench novelty. Keep water off the crown and leaves when irrigating, feed lightly every three to four weeks during active growth, and refresh plants periodically from leaf cuttings as older crowns decline.

common_name: Amethyst African Violet (Historic Original Ten Purple Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Amethyst was one of the original ten African violet selections released by Armacost & Royston, the California nursery credited with launching the species commercially in the United States.

directions: Propagate from leaf cuttings rooted in moist, well-drained mix, and grow the resulting plantlets as houseplants in bright indirect light in slightly acidic potting soil. Amethyst bears single flowers in a deep reddish-purple shade that stood apart from the more common blue tones among the earliest African violet introductions, set against a low rosette of fuzzy, dark green leaves. It shares the modest, unruffled flower form typical of the founding generation of cultivars, before decades of selective breeding introduced doubles, ruffles, and multicolor patterns. Water carefully at the soil line to avoid crown rot, feed lightly on a monthly schedule during the growing season, and divide or restart plants from cuttings as they age.

common_name: Commodore African Violet (Historic Original Ten Deep Violet Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Commodore was part of the original ten African violet cultivars distributed by Armacost & Royston in the late 1920s, launching the species' popularity in the United States.

directions: Grow from rooted leaf cuttings as a houseplant in bright, indirect light and slightly acidic, well-drained potting mix, keeping the crown dry when watering. Commodore produces single flowers in a deep, near-navy violet over a tidy rosette of dark, hairy foliage, a rich saturated shade among the handful of colors available when the species first entered commerce. Its straightforward, unfussy flower form and compact habit reflect its early place in African violet breeding history, well before ruffled edges and fantasy patterns became common. Feed lightly every three to four weeks during active growth and repot or divide every year or two to keep the rosette from becoming leggy.

common_name: Mermaid African Violet (Historic Original Ten Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Mermaid was one of the original ten African violet selections Armacost & Royston introduced to the American nursery trade in the late 1920s.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in a moist, well-drained propagating mix and grow the plantlets on as houseplants in bright, indirect light. Mermaid carries single, soft blue-violet flowers over a low rosette of dark green, fuzzy leaves, a lighter, more delicate tone than some of its original-ten counterparts and a color still echoed in modern pastel-blue African violet cultivars. It is grown today chiefly by collectors and African violet society members drawn to its place in the species' introduction to Western horticulture. Water at the soil line rather than overhead to protect the crown, and feed sparingly with a balanced African violet fertilizer during the active growing season.

common_name: Neptune African Violet (Historic Original Ten Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Neptune was among the original ten African violet cultivars released by Armacost & Royston, the nursery that first brought the species into American commerce.

directions: Propagate by rooting leaf cuttings in moist mix, then grow the resulting plants as houseplants in bright, indirect light and slightly acidic, well-drained potting soil. Neptune bears single, medium blue flowers with a slightly deeper throat over a compact rosette of dark, quilted foliage, a color that helped establish blue as the signature African violet hue long before pinks, whites, and bicolors joined the palette. Its simple form and modest size are typical of the founding generation of cultivars, now kept mainly for historical interest by collectors. Avoid wetting the leaves and crown when watering, feed lightly on a monthly cycle, and periodically restart plants from fresh leaf cuttings to maintain vigor.

common_name: Viking African Violet (Historic Original Ten Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Viking was one of the original ten African violet cultivars distributed by Armacost & Royston in the late 1920s as the species entered American horticulture.

directions: Root leaf cuttings in a moist propagating mix and grow the young plants on as houseplants in bright, indirect light, away from direct sun. Viking produces single, deep blue-purple flowers over a sturdy, well-filled rosette of dark green leaves, a robust grower among the original ten selections and one noted historically for its reliable, heavy bloom. It represents the plain, single-flowered form typical of African violets before ruffled edges, doubles, and fantasy patterns entered the breeding pool. Keep the crown dry when watering, feed lightly every three to four weeks in active growth, and divide congested clumps or restart from leaf cuttings as plants mature.

common_name: Tommie Lou African Violet (Variegated Tricolor Foliage Cultivar)

planting.note: Root leaf-stem cuttings in moistened propagating mix, selecting cuttings from well-variegated leaves; new plantlets emerge from the petiole base in 4-8 weeks. Tommie Lou is grown chiefly for its distinctive tricolor variegated foliage and has served as a parent for many later variegated-leaf African violet cultivars.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained potting mix, providing slightly stronger light than typical African violets to keep the variegation vivid. Tommie Lou is prized above all for its foliage, each leaf marked in irregular patches of green, cream, and pink, with semi-double lavender-blue flowers that are almost a secondary feature against the striking leaf pattern. Because variegation intensity can vary between individual leaves and cuttings, growers often select the most strongly patterned leaves when propagating to maintain a well-marked clone. Feed lightly and consistently, avoid overly warm, low-light conditions that cause the variegation to fade toward plain green, and remove any all-green reversion growth promptly to preserve the pattern.

common_name: Crystal Ice Streptocarpus (White Purple-Veined Cape Primrose)

planting.note: Divide crowded clumps or root leaf cuttings in spring; grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix. Crystal Ice is a popular white-flowered garden-center Streptocarpus valued for its crisp color contrast and free-flowering habit.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Crystal Ice bears crisp white flowers finely traced with purple veining radiating from a yellow-tinted throat, carried in generous clusters above a rosette of long, strap-shaped leaves. The strong contrast between the icy white petals and fine purple detailing makes it a standout among white-flowered Streptocarpus cultivars, and it flowers over a long season with good light. Deadhead spent flower stems at the base, feed lightly during active growth, and divide the rosette every couple of years to keep the clump compact and floriferous.

common_name: Polka Dot Purple Streptocarpus (AGM Spotted-Throat Cape Primrose)

planting.note: Divide crowded clumps or root leaf cuttings in spring; grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix. Polka Dot Purple holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable, heavy flowering and distinctive throat markings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, watering thoroughly and allowing the surface to dry before watering again. Polka Dot Purple carries rich violet-purple flowers marked with a dense scatter of dark spots deep in the throat, held in lax sprays over a rosette of long, textured leaves, a compact and exceptionally free-flowering form that earned it the RHS Award of Garden Merit. It flowers heavily over a long season and tolerates typical indoor conditions better than many showier hybrids. Remove faded flower stalks at the base to encourage continued bloom, feed lightly during active growth, and divide the clump every year or two to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Divide crowded clumps or root leaf cuttings in spring; grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix. Rosebud is grown for its unusual double, cupped flower form, distinct from the typical open-faced Streptocarpus bloom.

directions: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in slightly acidic, well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping the mix evenly moist but never waterlogged. Rosebud produces unusual double, tightly furled flowers that stay cupped rather than opening flat, resembling small rosebuds rather than the typical broad-faced Streptocarpus bloom, held above a rosette of long, quilted leaves. This distinctive flower form makes it a conversation piece among collectors even though its bloom count per stem is generally lighter than single-flowered cultivars. Deadhead spent stems at the base, feed lightly on a regular schedule during active growth, and divide the rosette periodically to keep the plant compact and productive.
